title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Aquarium maintenance
audience: Solo operators and team owners of aquarium maintenance businesses who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their route.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, tank type and repeat need.
Identify public signals that an aquarium need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the tank types you service well, such as freshwater home aquariums, planted tanks, marine systems, or display tanks in offices, and the price range you can sustain. Add the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A monthly round of tanks on a route you already run is worth far more to a small business than a single large job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. Marine work also needs its own criteria, because the fish and the rules for marine stock differ from freshwater.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. Pet and aquarium retailers are a prospect segment and a possible referral partner, because Queensland's fact sheet says unwanted fish go back to the retailer, to a new home, or are humanely destroyed (June 2020). Businesses with display tanks, such as offices, cafes and waiting rooms, are segments you can test. The research did not source them, so score them only on your own evidence. Add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Business.gov.au suggests a short profile for each segment (24 September 2024). Keep only business contact details that are published for business use. Do not use bought or harvested contact lists, because buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (ACMA, Spam Act obligations, 28 March 2019).

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that an aquarium need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. Examples include a new business fit-out with a display tank, a public tender for maintenance of tanks in a public building, and a body corporate notice of works to a common-area tank. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. Do not monitor private people, do not use personal information that is not public, and do not turn up at a home to make an offer. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders, and suppliers can set alerts (last updated 7 August 2026). Each state and territory runs its own tender system for local government and state work (business.gov.au, 19 August 2025). The research did not find a public signal specific to aquariums, so treat these as general signals to test.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It says how you came to know about the business or the work. It makes one specific observation that you can check from public view or from the business's own published material, such as a display tank that a business has listed with no maintenance named on its website. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined set of tanks or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found many approaches were pressured or misleading, and many salespeople did not identify themselves (28 July 2026). A specific, honest message that names you is therefore a practical advantage as well as a compliance step. Do not offer marine livestock or fish rehoming in outreach until you have checked the rule that applies.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them.

procedure: Write the tank type, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want, freshwater and marine separately.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the do-not-call rules for any call, and the fish rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: An aquarium business covers three suburbs in Sydney. A new cafe fit-out notice goes up in one of them, and the cafe's website lists a large display tank with no maintenance provider named. The cafe's general enquiries email address is published on the site.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message to the cafe now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should not send a sales email just because a business address is published. ACMA's Spam Act guidance says publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the owner first checks whether the cafe has agreed to receive them or has invited contact. If neither applies, the owner waits for an invitation or uses a route the cafe has agreed to. A phone call to a registered number is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, so the owner checks the register before calling. Any message that does go out names the fit-out, says how the business learned of it, observes that the website names no maintenance provider, offers one small next step such as a written quote for the display tank, and asks one question. The owner does not offer to rehome fish or to supply marine livestock unless the rule for that service has been checked.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, tank type and repeat need, with freshwater and marine kept separate
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Offering to sell, supply or rehome fish that the state or federal rules do not allow you to handle.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the fish and import rules before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state where the work is done requires. No aquarium maintenance licence was confirmed in any state. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Fish rules are state-based. Queensland says fish must not be released into waterways, wetlands or drains, and that selling prohibited or restricted fish on online marketplaces is illegal. New South Wales makes release and translocation illegal without a permit. Check the rule in each state before any outreach that mentions fish.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days (read 2026-11-03). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7, version dated 22 July 2019) says that public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

Telemarketing to registered numbers is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, which the DNCR industry guide (2018 copyright notice, older) describes as weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm. Check the register before any call.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the tank work you want first, freshwater and marine separately, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should an aquarium business contact first?
options: A one-off tank a long way outside your service area, because it looks large
A business with several display tanks inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows a fit-out with a display tank in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the business about the fit-out, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each employee using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for your tank service
Go into the premises to look at the tank before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

Do Not Call Register, 'DNCR industry guide', https://www.donotcall.gov.au/media/1212/dncr-industry-guide.pdf, 2018 copyright notice (older). Supports: telemarketing hours for registered numbers; lists must be washed against the register.

Gap: no aquarium-specific prospect, signal or referral figure was found. No aquarium fish-keeping club or aquarium society source was reached. Segments such as offices and cafes are not sourced and are to be tested.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: marketing messages need consent, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option honoured within five working days. Does not cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act, which the page says covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some other organisations. Small-business coverage and consent detail are unconfirmed here. Publisher: OAIC.
